newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore gas oil swaps unshaken by big IPE falls.
newsitem.headline: Singapore gas oil swaps unshaken by big IPE falls.

text.p: Singapore gas oil swaps were unfazed by the large falls to prices in the west as the market looked to latent regional demand for support, traders said on Friday.
"There is alot of buyers out there," one broker said. He said November swaps were already traded at $29.25 and $29.275 this morning.
November gas oil swaps was last quoted at $29.25/29.35, down a mere 30 cents from Thursday's close, brokers said.
In the west, November gas oil traded on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) plunged six percent or $13.75 per tonne to $225.00.
On NYMEX, heating oil closed at 3.05-cent less at 70.92 cents per gallon on news of a 1.3 million barrel rise in U.S. distillate stocks.
"Despite the big falls on the IPE, Singapore gas oil prices continue to lag the west," one trader said.
Gas oil prices in Singapore are currently about $7 per tonne below that quoted on the IPE, down sharply from a record $20.50 seen earlier this month.
But as prices in Singapore are still below that of the west, no arbitrage cargoes are expected to head to this region which should keep the market firm, traders said.
Traditionally prices in the east were higher than that of the west but this relationship changed recently following the startup of new refining capacities in Thailand and South Korea.
As a result, traders said players would continue to source their Africa requirements from the Middle East instead of the Mediterrenean--their previous source.
This would mean that spot Middle East exports to the east would remain scarce as was the case in September and October.
In addition to the limit on supplies, regional demand is the other component that is expected to keep prices stable, traders said.
Big consumers in China have shown recently that when it came to the crunch they are able to pay the high international prices for their gas oil, one trader said.
China in recent days bought cargoes for arrival in late October and early November at between $227 and $230 per tonne on a cost-and-freight basis.
On Thursday, buyers were bidding at up to $232 per tonne but sellers had backed off following the five-year record trade in Singapore at $30.00 per barrel free-on-board.
"Its not clear if China will continue to buy at these levels or whether they are going to lower their bids sharply (due to the big drop on the IPE)," one trader said.
But sources said barge lot business ex-terminal in Hong Kong was brisk and the majors there have imported more than 100,000-tonnes for arrival in October to meet this extra demand.
Ex-terminal prices in Hong Kong rose to trade at above $240 per tonne on Thursday.
Players said prices may not re-visit the five-year record mark in the near future due to the big drop in the west. But they welcomed the correction as it would spur buyers to return to the market.
--Singapore Newsroom (65-870-3093)
